text: Reading is thinking with some one else's head instead of one's own.
plain: When you only consume, you are borrowing someone else's brain.

text: The safest way of having no thoughts of one's own is to take up a book every moment one has nothing else to do.
plain: Filling every empty minute with input kills your own thinking.

text: Truth that has been merely learned is like an artificial limb, a false tooth, a waxen nose; at best, like a nose made out of another's flesh; it adheres to us only because it is put on. But truth acquired by thinking of our own is like a natural limb; it alone really belongs to us.
plain: What you only memorized sits on you. What you worked out yourself is part of you.

text: A man can always sit down and read, but not--think.
plain: Reading is easy to do on command. Real thinking is not.

text: Thinking must be kindled, like a fire by a draught; it must be sustained by some interest in the matter in hand.
plain: Good thinking needs a spark and something you actually care about.

text: A man should read only when his own thoughts stagnate at their source, which will happen often enough even with the best of minds.
plain: Read when you run dry, not to avoid thinking.

text: It is with thoughts as with men; they cannot always be summoned at pleasure; we must wait for them to come.
plain: You can't force ideas on schedule. Show up and let them arrive.

text: Not even the greatest mind is capable of thinking for itself at all times.
plain: Even the best minds have off hours. You are not broken.

text: To read another's thoughts is like taking the leavings of a meal to which we have not been invited, or putting on the clothes which some unknown visitor has laid aside.
plain: Secondhand ideas are leftovers and hand-me-downs. Make your own.

text: A library may be very large; but if it is in disorder, it is not so useful as one that is small but well arranged.
plain: Knowing a lot means little if it's a mess. Organize what you know.

text: The business of the novelist is not to relate great events, but to make small ones interesting.
plain: Craft is making ordinary things worth looking at.

text: If a man wants to read good books, he must make a point of avoiding bad ones; for life is short, and time and energy limited.
plain: Time is short. Cut the junk so the good stuff gets your attention.

text: The NEWSPAPER, is the second-hand in the clock of history; and it is not only made of baser metal than those which point to the minute and the hour, but it seldom goes right.
plain: The news is fast, cheap, and usually wrong.

text: Let us recognize that a newspaper is at best but a magnifying-glass, and very often merely a shadow on the wall.
plain: News blows things up or makes them up. Don't let it rule your mood.

text: The pen is to thought what the stick is to walking; but you walk most easily when you have no stick, and you think with the greatest perfection when you have no pen in your hand.
plain: Your best thinking happens before you grab the tool.

text: Human life is short and fleeting, and many millions of individuals share in it, who are swallowed by that monster of oblivion which is waiting for them with ever-open jaws.
plain: Millions live and vanish. Do something worth being remembered.

text: Every one who really thinks for himself is so far like a monarch. His position is undelegated and supreme.
plain: If you think for yourself, you answer to nobody's authority.

text: The source of all pleasure and delight is the feeling of kinship.
plain: We enjoy what feels like us. Find your people.

text: Does the worm see the eagle as it soars aloft?
plain: Small minds can't see high ones. Don't wait for them to understand you.

text: Contrarily, a reputation that is to last a long time must be slow in maturing, and the centuries of its duration have generally to be bought at the cost of contemporary praise.
plain: Lasting work is paid for by going unpraised for a long time.

text: There are two ways of behaving in regard to merit: either to have some of one's own, or to refuse any to others. The latter method is more convenient, and so it is generally adopted.
plain: Building your own worth is hard. Tearing down others is easy, and most people choose easy.

text: As envy is a mere sign of deficiency, so to envy merit argues the lack of it.
plain: Envy tells you what the envier lacks. Don't take it personally.

text: Men of great genius, whether their work be in poetry, philosophy or art, stand in all ages like isolated heroes, keeping up single-handed a desperate struggling against the onslaught of an army of opponents.
plain: Great people always stand nearly alone against the crowd.

text: When I watch the behavior of a crowd of people in the presence of some great master's work, and mark the manner of their applause, they often remind me of trained monkeys in a show.
plain: Crowd applause is often imitation, not understanding.

text: As a rule, people discover a man to be worth listening to only after he is gone; their hear, hear, resounds when the orator has left the platform.
plain: People applaud after you're gone. Don't wait on it.

text: As it is a rare thing for even one man out of many millions to tread the path that leads to immortality, he must of necessity be very lonely.
plain: A rare path is a lonely one. That's the price.

text: Meanwhile let me before all things recommend the traveler to take light baggage with him; otherwise he will have to throw away too much on the road.
plain: On a long road, carry less or you'll drop it all anyway.

text: Reverence cannot endure close proximity; it almost always dwells at some distance from its object; and in the presence of the person revered it melts like butter in the sun.
plain: Admiration fades up close. Nobody is a hero to those who see them daily.

text: When the facts themselves are eloquent of a truth, there is no need to rush to its aid with words: for time will give it a thousand tongues.
plain: If you're right, time will argue for you. Stop over-explaining.

text: As our emblem and coat of arms, I propose a tree mightily shaken by the wind, but still bearing its ruddy fruit on every branch; with the motto Dum convellor mitescunt, or Conquassata sed ferax.
plain: Get shaken by the storm and keep bearing fruit.

text: A man of learning is a man who has learned a great deal; a man of genius, one from whom we learn something which the genius has learned from nobody.
plain: Don't just collect knowledge. Produce something new.

text: He who wishes to experience gratitude from his contemporaries, must adjust his pace to theirs. But great things are never produced in this way.
plain: If you want applause now, you'll make average work. Move at your own pace.

text: What man has in any real sense lived more than he whose moments of thought make their echoes heard through the tumult of centuries?
plain: Real living is making something that outlasts you.

text: Great minds thus owe little ones some indulgence; for it is only in virtue of these little minds that they themselves are great.
plain: Be patient with smaller people. Greatness is measured against them.

text: It is often the case that a great mind prefers soliloquy to the dialogue he may have in this world.
plain: Sometimes your best company is your own head.

text: Great, genuine and extraordinary work can be done only in so far as its author disregards the method, the thoughts, the opinions of his contemporaries, and quietly works on, in spite of their criticism, on his side despising what they praise.
plain: Great work needs you to ignore what everyone else thinks and keep going.

text: Glory is such an uncertain thing, and, if you look at it closely, of so little value.
plain: Fame is flimsy. Don't build your life on it.

text: To read a philosopher's biography, instead of studying his thoughts, is like neglecting a picture and attending only to the style of its frame, debating whether it is carved well or ill, and how much it cost to gild it.
plain: Study the work and the ideas, not the gossip around them.

text: The mind of genius is among other minds what the carbuncle is among precious stones: it sends forth light of its own, while the others reflect only that which they have received.
plain: Be a source of light, not a mirror.

text: In order to have original, uncommon, and perhaps even immortal thoughts, it is enough to estrange oneself so fully from the world of things for a few moments, that the most ordinary objects and events appear quite new and unfamiliar.
plain: Original ideas come from seeing the ordinary as if for the first time.

text: To free a man from error is to give, not to take away. Knowledge that a thing is false is a truth.
plain: Losing a comforting lie is a gain, because you learn something true.

text: Error always does harm; sooner or later it will bring mischief to the man who harbors it.
plain: Believing something false always costs you in the end.

text: The truth, my dear sir, is the only safe thing; the truth alone remains steadfast and trusty; it is the only solid consolation; it is the indestructible diamond.
plain: Only truth holds up under pressure.

text: Hardly one in ten thousand will have the strength of mind to ask himself seriously and earnestly--is that true?
plain: Almost nobody asks whether what they believe is true. Be the one who does.

text: The flag to which I have taken the oath is truth; I shall remain faithful to it everywhere, and whether I succeed or not, I shall fight for light and truth!
plain: Pick truth as your flag and stay loyal whether you win or lose.
